review:
I genuinely love Prison Architect and I feel I've been patient with Paradox since their take over to give them a fair chance, but as of writing this, I have to recommend against this game now.

PA is a great building and management sim and, for the most part, still is. Far better than any "tycoon" game. Before the Paradox buyout, it had its problems, but they were minor, and while Paradox hasn't completely broken the game, they seem to have an annoying habit of just not thinking things through and taking two steps back for every step forward. While some things get fixed quickly (oversized boilers for example), others have not and others still are not bugs, but "upgrades" that hinder the player more than they help.

Paradox has introduced mostly new kinds of walls, floors, and objects to place. Nice and all, but ultimately superficial. On the flip side, they saw fit to change the deployment screen (where a great deal of prison planning is done) from a nice clear blue-print appearance with distinct solid colors, to a transparent overlay that makes colors difficult to distinguish. This change was never necessary and makes prison management harder to no benefit to the player whatsoever. The ability to "prioritize" patrol routes and designate armed guards to whole rooms instead of patrol paths is nice, but nothing we particularly needed.

In another case of "stop helping me" is the recent change to Protected Security AI which causes them to hide in their cells and not go anywhere that isn't exclusively designated protected security. While this makes some kind of sense, it's mostly a bother because now the handful of protected security prisoners you have require an entire mini-prison all to themselves to function when previously it was easy for me to let them mingle with non-violent minimum security prisoners, saving on space and expenses. The whole point of the game is to manage this stuff ourselves, not have the game trying to act like it knows better. It would have been more helpful if paroled prisoners and visitors obeyed the deployment settings instead.

In addition, I've heard the new DLC has been causing people to receive insane prisoners regardless if they have the DLC or not, and if they don't (or don't have it enabled) they are forced to deal with prisoners while having no access to the things those prisoners need. Furthermore, insane mothers can apparently appear and there is no cell in the game equipped to handle such a prisoner. While I haven't seen this particular bug myself, it's been reported on the forum many times and it does match up with other instances of the new dev team not thinking things through before implementing them. I didn't buy the game to do their QA job for them.

To anyone who picked up a copy of the game from Introversion's website directly: I recommend rolling back so you can continue to enjoy the game without gambling on Paradox's ineptitude to do so. 

Edit: As of 2025, changing my earlier "wait and see" recommendation to not recommended at all. From what I hear, Paradox's incompetence is a permanent thing. A sad fate for a once great game. I wouldn't put much faith in the sequel either, even if it manages to come out of being "indefinitely delayed."

Also, while I'm not one of those who absolutely hates the presence of the new launcher, it does strike me as unnecessary. It's just one more step where things can go wrong all so Paradox has a place to run ads - for the game we're already playing. We can go to the steam store page, thank you very much.

I love this game, but unfortunately I just can't recommend it in it's current state, and I don't think it'll get better. The game is a buggy mess and the developers have no interest in fixing the game. The only reason they patch the game is when they have some over-priced content-lacking "expansion" that they can tack onto the game. Bugs go months without being fixed, bugs that should be patched within days. Currently canned drinks, a luxury item that prisoners can purchase, are currently considered contraband. This should be a single-line fix, and yet it's been over 2 months. This is very typical. 

They don't ever improve existing aspects of the game, they just duct tape and flood the outdated UI with more crap. Nothing has any consistency, rhyme, or reason. The UI is just filled with random stuff, DLC items tacked onto existing menus, random tabs and buttons in random places. 

The larger your prison gets, the worse the game becomes. There's an achievement for having 1,000 prisoners, so they clearly intended for you to be able to create large prisons, but the game makes it nearly unplayable. After 750~ prisoners, the frame-rate and performance basically gives up. When the performance drops, the game becomes incredibly hard to control the game. Everything becomes laggy, and your clicks/selections will stop registering. Sometimes it takes 5-6 clicks for it to register, it's incredibly frustrating. You are basically forced to pause time if you want to do anything - it's the only way to control things at that point. That's not even mentioning the connections or energy menus, those are laggy no matter how many prisoners you have. It can be ridiculously hard to use because it lags so much.

That's not even scratching the surface of the problems in this game. There's so much to go over - it's just exhausting. The game is fun, but they've neglected it so much while still slapping on random ideas that don't make sense for the setting (and they probably stole the idea from a free mod) 

Unfortunately, I don't see this game getting any better. These have been problems with the game for years, and people have been begging for fixes the entire time. They have no care for the game, any 'care' they feign is just so that they can try and trick people into buying the new pointless DLC expansions that break more of the game. (That they won't fix) 

I seriously recommend looking for a different game - I've heard good things about Rim World.

Despite this being my second most played game on Steam and one of my favorites, it breaks my heart to have to leave it a negative review. Around a year ago, the original developer, Introversion Software, sold Prison Architect to Paradox Interactive. Unfortunately, Paradox has ruined the original integrity and quality of the game. They have already pumped out 2 DLCS, both of which are absolutely filled with bugs, the dlc's aren't even spectacular on their own. Both of them are small updates that add very little reason to actually purchase them. As if that wasn't bad enough, Paradox has added very few actual good additions to the game through the free updates. The updates are basically just a few new wall patterns and a floor. And, while Paradox has added a few good additions to the game, specifically quality of life changes, they just don't care enough to fix more than 10% of the bugs in the game, and each new update only adds more. They added a launcher, which doesn't seem like a big deal at first, just useless. Until you realize that they fill the launcher up with ads for Paradox's other games, it's less that it gets in your way and more that it's just insulting to players of the game, especially long time ones. They have shown themselves to have no intention of listening to the players, continuing to ignore practically every piece of criticism. Do not purchase this game if you're looking for a game with constant updates and a developer who has any ounce of quality control.

Even after 1,800 hours, I sometimes discover interesting new things that are not always mentioned in the game description, campaign mode (tutorial), or online wikis. These include:
[list]
    [*] when carefully watching the prisoners for a while, one of them may briefly flash a contraband item they are trying to discreetly hold, and it can then be confiscated with a search
    [*] prisoners can rummage through trash bins for contraband (by briefly moving on top of it)
    [*] drunk prisoners bump into walls and struggle to walk in a straight line; high prisoners walk with erratic bursts of speed
    [*] guard dogs maul prisoners to death in revenge if said prisoner has killed the guard dog owner
    [*] given the opportunity, prisoners will always attempt to pick up dropped jail keys before the guards remove them
    [*] prisoners attempting to escape will skid across the pavement if tased or knocked unconscious while making a run for it
    [*] maximum security and legendary prisoners have the ability to occasionally break free of handcuffs while in lockdown/solitary
    [*] max-sec and legendary prisoners are also much more likely to spontaneously attack a weak staff member (janitors, gardeners, chefs, teachers, and spiritual leaders) if the staff member has the misfortune of walking too close to them
    [*] actively rioting prisoners are essentially immortal (to starvation) unless tased, knocked unconscious, or killed; they are able to riot indefinitely if left alone and will not starve to death even with the "starving" status effect
    [*] released prisoners have all their status effects frozen and cannot starve to death, pee/poo themselves, go to classes, etc, even if trapped in your prison forever
    [*] prisoners are willing to travel quite far (sometimes across entire cell blocks) to attack a snitch or confidential informant
    [*] very rarely, a family visiting a prisoner in visitation will make the prisoner angry, and the prisoner will attempt to kill their family members
    [*] Idle prisoners and staff will sometimes close their eyes after a while as if dozing off, or sniffle and sneeze
    [*] in escape mode on the console version, there is a special friendly immortal guard called Karl the Cop who helps open doors for you
[/list] 

10/10 would recommend if obsessed with small details and watching prisoners smack each other with garden shears.

The Campaign (which also serves as the tutorial) opens with a prison that isn't quite finished yet. And you are told by your boss, the CEO of the "For Profit" Prison, that you have been given the task of executing a murderer. And this order comes from the state itself.

The game then turns towards teaching you how to work the basic construction tools, explaining power, water, foundations, interior walls, and room basics in a straightforward and clean manner.

Then the game shows you exactly why your prisoner is guilty.

It is not a pleasant experience to watch as a tiny cartoon man walk into his home, find his tiny cartoon wife fucking a tiny cartoon stranger in his bed, and then tearfully shoot them both in the head.

This gives us the biggest lesson of all: Prison Architect is not a happy game.

Prison Architect is a top down management game where you run your prison company exactly how you want it. As far as the state is concerned, it doesn't matter how high your rehabilitation rate is, all that matters is that you have no escapes, keep the deaths to an acceptable low, and you keep the prisoners in line by any means you deem fit.

Once you finish your campaign, which takes you through the systems of the game, explaining core concepts quite happily while also telling you tales of loss, pain, murder, ambition, hope, and sheer murderous rage. Of course, the problem is that the game ONLY explains the core mechanics and leaves more complicated ones for you to figure out yourself. That said, while there is a Wiki and many a guide for you, the point of the core game in sandbox mode is mostly to see what works best. To adapt to problems and overcome even of it must be done through trail, error and blood.

The game provides security measures such as cameras, remote doors opened by a button or a timer, stab vests and tazers for your guards, and even heavily armed maximum force response teams kept on site with shotguns, full body armor, and the will and means to paint your prison red with blood at your command. Along with this the game will provide schedules, assignments, patrols, and even resticted acess zoning, all of which is designed to keep your prisoners under control so they do not kill each other.

Along with this is provided many means to turn your prisoners into peaceful members of society if you so choose. You may provide basic education, as many prisoners lack even a child's reading and writing skills. And some of them cannot even read at all, let alone write. Give your prisoners trade skills as carpenters or metal workers. Teach them how to be cleaners or work a laundry. And then set up security systems to prevent prisoners stealing hammers or making crude knives.

Prisoners may come with medical issues such as addiction, alchoholism or violent pshycological instability. Build a common room for AA meetings, an office for one on one meetings for professional mental help, an infirmary for chemical treatmeants to help with addiction and minor surgery when the prisoners try to kill, and a mourge when they do kill.

Your prisoners are humans, with desires and needs, thoughts and feelings, and intelligence. Prisoners need to be fed, and you may give them things to do. Build a common room with tables, television sets, and phones. Provide meals at preset times, as many times as you want, in large quantaties and variety if you want, or a simple bowl of vegetable soup once a day if you don't. Prisoners with many things to do are less likey to cause trouble, and giving them these things may make them very happy indeed.

This does not mean you may treat them like sane members of society. You are running a prison. They are prisoners. And Prisoners are not in the habit of obeying the rules. Prisoners steal, fight, and even kill in your walls. Make no mistake, you and your officers are the only order inside the prison. Without your constant watchful gaze and omnipresent guards the prisoners will fall upon each other like wild animals; killing, fighting, and breaking.

If your prisoners are exceptionally angry, and if your prison is weak enough, the prisoners may decide that they can do whatever thy want and there is nothing you can do about it. They may decide to riot. Or you may subdue them, show them that any antisocial behaviour will not be tolerated, and make them docile through fear.

Problems may arise in your prison, and of course these are optional. Make it so that he game throws problems your way at random. Maybe a highly contagious disease is rampaging through your prison and killing your prisoners. Perhaps a water main has burst. Maybe a generator has overloaded, causing a fire and a blackout. Or maybe the mayor has bowed to political pressure and decided to implement reform without consulting you.

If you feel particularly brave, allow the game to generate gangs, and watch as your prison becomes split by three gangs into territories, and attempt to usurp your authority. And then spiral into gang wars, burn your prison down, kill your guards, and extort prisoners.

Prison Architect, ultimately, is exactly what it says it is, with a remarkable and well made game that most will like.  BUt do not expect to laugh because of the cutesy graphics. 

They mitigate the horror, but only make it bearable.

I was several hours into my first game of Prison Architect when I found myself humiliated. I'm talking genuine, utter, red-faced humiliation, complete with a trickle of perspiration and a vaguely sick feeling in the pit of my gut. I've been humiliated plenty of times in online games, but this was an entirely new experience for me in single-player.

I'd been playing Introversion Software's prison construction and management simulator the same way I play any other sim, by slowly expanding my network of buildings—cells, rec rooms, storage closets, administrative offices—while keeping an eye on my finances, staff, and current goals. Most of all, I'd been doing everything I could to meet the needs of my ever-growing population of inmates. If they complained about being hungry, I'd expand the kitchen, serve higher quality meals, and allow more time on their schedules for chow. If they complained about hygiene, a lack of recreation options, or that they missed their families, I'd stop everything and construct new facilities or activate new prisoner programs to accommodate them. As a result of this close attention I'd experienced no riots, no fist-fights, no unpleasantness of any kind. Everything seemed to be going great.

Then I received a notification that an escape tunnel had been found. Five prisoners in adjoining cells had smuggled in tools and burrowed to freedom right under my nose (and right under the prison's exterior wall). I immediately felt betrayed. I'd been bending over backwards to meet their needs, to run a clean, efficient, and extraordinarily humane prison. How could they do this to me? That's when the embarrassment hit, because something important and incredibly obvious simply hadn't dawned on me until that very moment: meeting an inmate's needs isn't the same thing as making them happy. Prison Architect isn't like other management sims where you deal with a restless and fickle population. There simply is no happy state for your residents. Maybe they don't want to start fires or lay into a guard with a power drill, but that doesn't mean they actually want to be there. It's prison. It's right in the title. No one wants to be there! Lesson learned, too late.

I whole heartedly recommend this game.  At the time of review I have 210 hrs of game time in.  Far behind in my library at #2 is Kerbal Space Program with 105.  This game is perfectly paced, completely open to infinite designs and has so much depth I can easily see hitting 500hrs.  After the latest update (alpha 31) this game is packed with content and the workshop offers massive expansion and awesome mods (Imperial architect being my current fav.  Star wars prison!).

Pros:
As big as you wanna be!  Want to make a small 25 person prison  that runs efficiently and makes money with minimum security bluecollar criminals?  Go ahead!  Want to make a 500 person Max security only iron curtain that can hold and control intensely volatile and psychotic madmen?  Sure can!

Well designed!  The UI and indicators for things like prison heat, tech tree, controlling and managing intake and regime of the inmates and hiring and firing staff, as well as prison programs is easy to understand and impliment.  I've played plenty of games that after opening them up and fiddling with for 20 minutes I can hardly make heads or tails of the UI or it has infinitely frusturating menus to navigate or item info to memorize.  Not so with PA. 

Entertaining!  Set up phone taps and learn a prisoner has set up a time for someone to throw booze over the wall into the garbage area?  Watch them toddle over into the area and as they head back inside stop them and counter their contraband!  Initiate shakedowns to find inmates who have dummys in their beds and are digging tunnels!  The excitement of unearthing a tunnel they have been digging for days that NEARLY reached the outside but was thwarted is always satisfying.  Recruit confidential informants to reveal persons who have knives, needles, poison SHOTGUNS in their cells.  Use sniffer dogs to inspect incoming food and items to ensure they are poison and piano wire free.  The combinations and implications are endless.

No two prisons are ever the same!  One prison may be full of raging alcoholics, another may be a mix of volatile angry inmates and ex law enforcment or snitches that must be contained and seperated or death ensues!  My last prison had 3 legendary prisoners, each capable of disarming and killing guards in a single punch.  Not only must you constantly learn to streamline your prison and improve every aspect of the design you also have to adapt and keep tabs on your current and incoming prisoners, keeping the troublemakers at bay and keeping your staff running smoothly.

Cons:

Still early access.  This isnt necessarily a con but something to be take into consideration.  This game has all the content and playability and optimization of a full release but as new features ar implimented new bugs invariably creep up.  In the most recent patch my cooks tend to randomly pile dirty trays in the cells of my supermax and solitary prisoners.  Later in the day they pick them up and wash them.  On occasion I will assign a block to eat in a specific canteen, and then assign a specific kitchen to feed them.  Later on suddenly I will check my prisoners needs and some are starving.  I will check my food distribution screen and randomly the kitchen and canteen to cellblock link is totally gone.  Its not perfect, but none of these bugs or issues are anywhere near game breaking and are fairly smalltime.

In conclusion get this game.  The developers are awesome, the game is amazing, and its not even complete yet!  I look forward to future updates and features and the workshop community is actively making new mods regularily that add even more to the experience.  98/100

EDIT: 9/19/2018

This game is still getting updates and is the pinnacle of variety and easily makes my personal top 10 games ever created.  With workshop integration and countless additions since my last review if you don't own this game by now buy it!

Where do I begin with a game like this. Well for starters this game was made by an indie company, no big publisher backing Introversion, they have done an amazing job getting this game to where it is at this time. In short, buy this game it is an amazing experience.

For those who wish to read, I will now go over the pros and cons of this game in detail.

Pros:

Build just the way you want:

There are very few contraints when building. I'd liken it to Sims 3 from a top down perspective in terms of building. It's great fun.

Cartoony but realistic at the same time:
The game has a very distinctive art style that is unique to the game, but it deals with serious topics such as if you will execute a death row prisoner or not, or if you will keep a prisoner locked up for virtually all of his day. This game makes you think.

It's tough, but only if you want it to be/You can go at your own pace:
The aim of the game is not to amass one billion dollars, but to have the lowest reoffending rate for released prisoners, and every in game day can be marginally relaxing if you want it to. For instance you can run a low-security, generally free environment where the aim is to rehabilitate your prisoners through the use of classes you can run, or you can run a max-sec environment punishing the most hardcore of criminals. It's all up to you.

A dedicated team:
I have watched nearly every alpha video that has been published, and I can clearly see that Introversion software is very passionate about the project. There were (As of writing this it's about a day off offical release) new features each month, and it was a pleasure to watch each and every video.

If you enjoyed Sim City you'll love this. There are features very soon to be released I haven't gone over yet,  as well as features I missed,but you'll see for yourself.

Cons:

Somewhat gruelling at the start:

After putting a good 200 hours into the game as a whole, this is probably my most major complaint with the game, is that in the beginning you start with 30K and the only way you can make money is via grants, but selling your first prison is practically the only way to make cash when you're still learning the ropes.

Overall a solid 8.5/9 out of 10, certainly one of the best sim and strategy/managment games I have ever played. For $30 you will get a lot of fun out of this. Strongly recommended.

Years ago, I worked in a prison... Northern nevada Correction Center and Warm Springs Correctional Center located in Carson City Nevada. That being said, a few games have come out over the years trying to emulate running a prison. Prison Tycoon 1 & 2 were the first that I tried. Both failed miserably. This game has a long way to go, but it is trying... improving... and actually comes close. Riots, gang wars, contraband, escapes and even a death row. Real rehabilitation, if there is such a thing. Not all inmates go back to prison whatever the reason.

This game is evolving, getting better and feels real on some levels.

A critical review should be just that, critical. So while I give this game a thumbs up, it is not perfect. It has bugs, Some new, some old, but many are recognized and others have been fixed. The developers are working to improve it both in game play and fixing that which is broken. I have not seen a game breaking bug.

An active community of posted prisons and mods, the spread of ideas and again active developers have made this game more real than it's predicessors and a bit fun.

My 1 suggestion is to add race tension. Race wars are alive and well in the US prisons. Segregation could be implemented as it is in many prisons. However, Gangs do add an interesting aspect that mimic this, but recruitment is rampant in prisons and should be added as well. Gun towers, a better way to implement sally ports (1 door can not open until the other closes, linking doors together in some way of added user defined rules) and so forth. How about a bit of staff corruption? All of this would make the game more real, challenging and fun.

Early Access done right. One of very few examples of such a phenomenon. From the communications the devs had with the community through both written and video updates, to the constant patching of the game which added significant changes and additions at an incredibly effective pace.

Truly, this game deserves your attention even if you're not interested in its gameplay mechanics or ideas. Simply because we ought to support this kind of transparent, respectful and talented videogame development. We need to show the rest of the industry that hard work and good communication is in the end rewarded.

Oh yeah, and the game itself is of course really good. It's like a more complex and more free-form version of Theme Hospital, chock full of intentional and unintentional humor. It's virtually replayable ad infinitum due to the smart integration of really complex systems and mechanics that are still simple enough to get a basic grasp on quickly. 

And then you add the solid Steam Workshop integration that's already been out for months and months, molding into a vast web of minor tweaks and major total convention mods to further extend your playtime. Like the mod that lets you take control of a prisoner, and use the game's own mechanics to try and break out of your own (or someone else's) prison! How genius is that?!

You could pay all the salary you're ever going to earn in your entire life, and you'd STILL be able to get a whole lot of bang for your buck with Prison Architect. And I'm not even sure if that's an exaggeration.

I don't think anyone wakes up in the morning and goes "I want to build a prison today." Penitentiaries just don't have the same feel-good appeal as cultivating a city or a business, really. The developers behind Prison Architect clearly had this in mind the whole way through development, because every manner of mishap and tragedy that can happen in a prison can happen here. However, they wrapped it up in such a wealth of building options that you won't even have time to question the ethics of your creations.

Prison Architect drops you off on a flat piece of land with a road running through it, and expects you to build a house of corrections. You're given an initial grant of money and some builders, and from that humble beginning you build cells, showers, kitchens, offices, power plants, laundry rooms, exercise yards, chapels, armories, morgues, classrooms... Honestly I don't have enough space to list out all the facilities you can place. The big selling point behind PA that will become immediately obvious is that you can build EVERYTHING. No detail is spared in how the prison is simulated, and every phone booth and ironing board must be accounted for.

This incredible level of detail extends to your prisoners and the handling of them, as well. Each of your little ne'er-do-wells has a detailed rap sheet and biography, specific incarceration needs including security level, moods and interests, and a laundry list of stats that can be tracked. Of course, you can't just throw such complex sims in a hole and call it a day (okay you can but it won't end well). Your prisoners have a schedule to stick to that includes eating, showering, working, playing, and sleeping. You can edit this schedule to your heart's content, even setting different schedules for different security levels.

There's still a boatload of systems I haven't even touched on like advanced security and visitation and work programs and research, but surely you get the point by now. Understand that while all this may sound daunting, Prison Architect handles it in a very gentle way. Early on, prisons don't need hardly any of the complex amenities, giving you time to unlock and familiarize yourself with them. You also have a huge list of options for customizing your difficulty, allowing you to even disable certain systems if you feel they make the game too complex. It's a consideration that more in-depth sims should adopt, because it means casual players and experienced managers can all find a pace they enjoy.

It's rare to find such a deep and detailed simulation that also allows you to dive just as far as you want, and at your own pace. You can tool along with a mostly functional prison just with the basic food and shelter services, explore additional systems at your pace, or go whole-hog in an attempt to build the perfect penitentiary. The 2D vector graphics might not be the most attractive but their simple lines and animations help keep the detailed interactions of your prison clear. Sound design is admittedly minimal, but it's not much of a drawback when there's so much more offered. No matter your skill or interest level, Prison Architect will find a way to capture your attention.

Prison architect is a prison simulator with a grid building system and an in depth prisoner needs system. 

Prison architect starts with the player immediately thrown into the game with hardy any tutorial. The real tutorial is the campaigns objectives. Once the player starts a game, they start with a small sum of money and must build a prison with the tools at their disposal. The player will build buildings for various rooms such as dormitories, cells, canteens, staff rooms, storage and other such necessities for the future prisoners and staff. 

The prisoners come in all shapes and sizes, as well as various security levels; minimum, medium and high security. These prisoners act like real prisoners, if there is a shortage of food, a heat wave, power outages, or even a death can cause a riot to break out. Prisoners can be kept happy by having visitation rooms, recreational rooms, time in the yard, or an increase in variety of food. Should a riot break out, riot police and firefighters are available to help put them back in line, and medical centres or morgues are available for the wounded or fatalities. 

Prison architect also has variety of options available when starting anew map, you can have weather as a factor, chose to have a large or small starting map, with our without trees, lakes or pre-existing buildings. Events are an interesting option, which can range from a power generator exploding, or a massive amount of prisoners arriving from another prison. Gangs can be turned on, which makes riots happen often, and if a gang leader is sent to your prison, the gangs can increase in size, and have wars over territory. Fog of war seems to be the most notorious of options. It prevents the player from seeing any prisoner unless a guard or camera is in the room, making it difficult, for the player to spot assaults or other such crimes. 

Overall prison architects objective is to rehabilitate prisoners through reform programs, such as school, culinary or workshop programs. These, if passed, provide the prisoner with valuable work skills reducing the chance of reoffending, boosting your prison grade.

As you can tell by my hours in this game, I have some experience with it, so I wanted to put forward my thoughts and the parts of the game available for anyone unsure about it. 

The Prison:
The game is obviously a simulator for building and running your prison, which can go terribly or great depending on how you take the situation and manage your funding (unless you use unlimited funding) and the rehabilitation or punishment of the prisoners. I personally enjoy the bird's eye-view layout and building system, offering a simple and flexible way for you to plan out your constructions. The various planning of your prison allows for you to make what you deem is fitting placement for your prisoners and staff, or at least what you can afford for your prison. 
In addition to multiple buildings, rooms and workshops available to the prisoners, you can also offer programs, changes to the regime and policies to crime and where prisoners can and cannot go. This effects the prison and keeps money coming in as well as keeping prisoners in line. This makes for an easier time for the prison and keeps your playtime from simply overlooking issues as well as protecting those vulnerable to gangs and crime. 

Prisoners: 
 Prison Architect offers a variety of named characters, some being various random NPCs, some you will glance over and see nothing, mainly those in minimum and normal security levels, yet you will find that those in higher levels you will learn the definite troublemakers and gang leaders if you toggle the option. I personally have a policy of those who committed murder in or out the prison go to Supermax, where most act within the rules but two of the three gang leaders are placed in there, causing much trouble for my prison and their punishment ends in other gang members becoming angry. Prisoners themselves have their own attitudes to the prison, staff, other prisoners and their own problems with addictions to drugs and alcohol. You also have access to the 'Names in game' option in extras, where you may select of the many player or dev made characters with some harrowing stories written by the sickos that enjoy the game and I love importing the funny and interesting characters made by people. Many of these taken from all sorts of games, history or just named after their creator, many having influence and fame in my prison, such as Dracula (who is a drug trafficker) and Stalin who has become a gang member and plays into murders. Unfortunately even with the stories written and customisation, you cannot dictate how your character will act in the prisons they are imported to, which would make your character much more recognisable and funny, especially with some of the amazing short tales made by people and could be tailored to causing trouble or being one who will help get rid of those troublemakers. With the more gameplay, the more responsibility you have if you wish to take it on for more money or a more interesting savegame, such as the act of imprisoning Death Row prisoners and the execution. .

I've already mentioned the programs and regime, which directly effects how your prisoners live and act. As the Architect you may play how you wish and your play goes in some respects. You may offer work or programs to different security levels, which you should be wary of employing the violent or long-serving prisoners, or put in place metal detectors to stop prisoners smuggling tools for escape or weaponry back to their cell or into the communal areas where they can attack other prisoners and gain renown / fame in your prison. Gangs will target those with high notoriety for violence or those you would look over to smuggle goods throughout the prison. I personally play into an idea of more privileges for those in the lesser securities or protective custody being cut off from the rest of the prison. This is mostly due to violent prisoners wanting to attack and possibly kill those you should put in protective, such as snitches, ex-law enforcement or those attacked often. 

I love this idea of acting to keep the prisoners in line or if you wish to see some violence, put them in one security together and just...reduce the number of guards in the area. If you love playing around with situations, play with cheats and unlimited funds. Unfortunately I have found the game simply crashes or bugs if a situation you have manufactured or come across occurs, such as my personal annoyance at two Gang leaders getting placed in the same Dormitory, where I locked them both in by walls so guards cannot interfere and have them stuck until one killed the other, which would start a gang war and make an interesting situation of the prison to watch. Yet when one of the gang leaders died, the game crashed and refused to continue, which obviously made a game that is a sandbox less fun and open. I have also found riots to be potentially amazingly fun or terrible for crashes and bugs. 

Management:
The game also allows you to place patrols, deployment and security measures in the prison to stop the prisoners from ruling over your prison for you. In addition you can employ confidential informants to help you know exactly where contraband and deliveries are happening, but be careful how much you use one individual, as prisoners will start to become suspicious to how much this one is being taken away and who is getting found out randomly. If the suspicion becomes too high, the prisoner may be known as a snitch and be a target for the violent prisoners to kill in the places where guards may not see or get to in time. 

Mods:
Many mods have been made for the graphical interests from players, such as Star Wars, World War two or more modernised military depending on your interest. Players have also made mods to help with some small issues that have not been fixed by the devs, such as prisoners being able to sit on their bed and read instead of needing to have a chair in their cell. However, I have found most of the time, especially with more time invested in the prison, that the game reacts harshly to the mods and crashes frequently or in certain situations, such as the Star Wars mod crashing when you have a riot. Personally I don't touch any mods anymore after many crashes at certain points.

Issues:
Many issues come with this game, such as the crashes and overlooked bugs that generally come later in a save and when you have invested time into it, which makes it certainly more frustrating. I have found at some points the game constantly crashes in my longer save games and makes it much more difficult for an enjoyable experience. However in some of my prisons I have had much fewer crashes than others. I also found what causes more crashes in the death of many NPCs, such as riots or shooting prisoners and makes it annoying when you sometimes cannot stop a riot from happening, meaning you can't stop a crash. 

Personally, the main good things I feel about the game:
- Freedom of creation and how the prison looks and feels.
- Prisoner stories, personalities, traits and gang affiliation. 
- The multiple ways you can tackle crime within your prison, be it informants, armed guards or rehabilitation.

Drawbacks and failings of the game:
- Programmed in issues which you cannot get rid of, such as Gang leaders as already mentioned as well as some contraband getting in even with you continuously searching and stopping goods from getting in through watching delivery areas. This makes it much more gamelike and constantly brings issues for you. 
- Lacking customisation of characters and personality. 
- Crashes, over small mods or things that you want to do, limiting your options for each save. 

I do recommend this game, yet I will recommend caution when using this game and the level of crashes is disgusting for those who enjoy playing one save to try get to a high prisoner count. The Safemode does not fix this and I personally think the devs need to fix this before I can 100% recommend this game completely.

Prison Architect was once a genuinely fun and addictive game. Unfortunately, Paradox Interactive took over after its original release and has since treated it like many of its other titles: squeeze as much money as possible out of the player base through an endless stream of DLCs while leaving serious bugs unfixed.

Anyone familiar with Paradox's business model knows exactly what that means. Players get milked like cows, with content split into countless paid expansions—sometimes for additions as laughably small as different uniform colors. Meanwhile, the actual game becomes increasingly unstable.

One particularly infuriating bug regularly causes employees to get stuck in the staff room while holding food trays near the serving tables. They simply stand there indefinitely instead of eating, resting, or returning to work. Once enough staff members get stuck, essential parts of the prison stop functioning properly. The result is a management game in which your prison can collapse not because of poor planning, but because the staff AI is completely broken.

There is no reliable permanent fix. You can move furniture, rebuild rooms, change layouts, remove serving tables, or create separate staff canteens, but these are temporary workarounds at best. The bug eventually returns. A game that depends entirely on working pathfinding, staff behavior, and resource management becomes borderline unplayable when employees repeatedly freeze while carrying food trays.

I previously said that Prison Architect itself was still worth playing despite Paradox's increasingly obvious cash-grab business model. At this point, I can no longer recommend it. A good game has been buried under DLCs, technical problems, and bugs that should have been fixed long ago.

So thank you, Paradox, for taking a good game and making it practically unplayable. But hey, at least you managed to release a pile of DLCs and charge players for every tiny addition while the basic game mechanics continue to break.

[h1]TL:DR? See Conclusion[/h1]

[h1]NOTE:[/h1] As an Early Access Review, this will be subjected to change and editing as newer updates are released.

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
Prison Architect is a 2D top down prison building and management simulation game made by Introversion Software being financed by crowd-funding, pre-orders and Steam Early Access. Since it's initial release on 2012, the game has undergone several major updates (an average of 4 weeks per update) and has raised nearly $10 Million in revenue.

[h1]PLOT (No Spoiler):[/h1]
The player takes on the role of a Prison owner, architect and governor who's objective is to create a prison from an expandable open world map. The player may choose the purpose of their prison either focused on reforming criminals, severe draconian punishment, or a mix of the two. Build the prison from scratch, hire guards and officers, staff and maintenance crew to keep it functioning, dog patrols to keep watch and many more. There is no end to the game, the player just needs to keep building and keep expanding until they decide to sell their prison and build a new one, or, have it burned to the ground because of a riot and find yourself in prison (seriously, your character can go to jail if you're grossly negligent in its management, ironically, in the same prison you built).

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Great 2D Art Style
+ Good Tutorial: Comprehensive and easy to understand
+ Vast variety of Characters (Staff, Officers, Prisoners, Guards etc)
+ Expanding World Map: (Buy the adjacent lot to expand)
+ Detailed Micromanagement System (Prisoner Regime, Guard/Dog Patrols, lock downs etc.)
+ Detailed Construction System (Buildings, water systems, electrical wiring, computer controls etc.)
+ Easy to install and uninstall MODS (Steam Workshop)
+ [url=https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCuWAgvyiWcBeZ8sT0sJZyBg]Monthly Updates from the devs[/url]
+ Old Computer friendly
+ High Replayability

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- Severe Performance Drop when the prison becomes very large (in size, prisoner and staff)
- Lacking in Soundtracks
- Occasional path-finding problems
- No main menu (minor annoyance and not a deal breaker)
- No Steam Cloud Support
- Prisoners are released Naked sometimes

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
GREAT EARLY ACCESS GAME. Prison Architect is what all Early Access games should try to be; it has constant updates, great art style, solid core gameplay, stable & playable and most importantly, easy on the pocket even at full price.

[h1]WORTH IT?:[/h1]
MUST TRY, whether the game is at full price or sale, it's worth every penny and I fully RECOMMEND it specially if your a City Building / Simulation fan. To be honest, the game is technically finished in my opinion (just need a bit more bug fixing and performance improvements) and has more features than some of the other fully released games I've seen.

Before I start, let me just say that this game is 100% worth the price. I bought this game several years back and despite it being a bit rough around the edges in places I've enjoyed it every time I played it. However, if my word alone isn't enough to convince you to buy this, here's the longer review, prepare for a lot of reading.

Firstly, the really compelling part of this game is the sheer amount of complexity of it's systems. every single system acts logically within the game world and interacts logically with the other systems. Introversion could have just let you place a "Library" room and made prisoners fulfill their education needs when they stand in it, but instead, if you want a library you have to place it, furnish it, wait for workers to place said furniture, train prisoners through school work, staff said prisoners in the library, sort through all of the books, let prisoners borrow those books and take them back to their cells, etc... This attention to detail permeates every mechanic in the game, and you can tell that Introversion really put their heart and soul into developing it.

Secondly, I should talk about the aspects of this game that leave a little to be desired. Most of it boils down to a simple lack of polish but it's still worth mentioning here. I've encountered numerous graphical bugs and glitches throughout my time playing, and even though the graphics themselves are passible, they still leave a lot to be desired. The UI can feel a bit clunky at times, but after a while you'll get used to it. Some of the experimental map settings like water and derelict buildings never really seem to work for me without mods, and they just tend to make the game less fun even when they generate well. Maybe that's just me but it still needs to be said. Also, escape mode in the game is really just a joke. It's kind of novel at first to try to escape from the prison's you've built, but it gets very dull very fast. However, so long as you don't see escape mode as an actual game mode, but instead as a fun little add on that you'll try once or twice and never use again, you won't be very disapointed. All in all, it seems like most of the flaws in this game just seem to stem from a lack of polish, but because of the size of the team involved and the robustness of the rest of the game I'm very quick to forgive Introversion for the few gripes I do have with the game.

Finally, I need to touch on the theme that this game represents. To say it bluntly, this game is dark. You won't notice it at first, because other than the campaign and the death row system there is nothing overtly depressing or sad in this game. However, after you've played several hours you might take a step back and realize that those little sprites on the screen represent human people that you are keeping locked up for (In game) years at a time. Introversion had two ways to go with this theme, they could've just not bothered with it or they could use their game to convey a message, and they chose the latter. In the game you can either treat your prisoners poorly or you can treat them well. Being the good samaritan I am, on my first playthrough I decided that I wanted to treat them well. I gave my prisoners all the amenities that they wanted and made sure that they were happy and healthy. However, despite this making me feel good it also left me bankrupt, and the biggest way to make money in the game is to take on more prisoners, so I did. Eventually though, this turned my nice little prison into a living hell. I overcrowded the limited space I had, and because of that fights broke out, not enough prisoners had access to the amenities that I provided, which sent their needs down, and both my reoffending rate and my murder rate went through the roof. Pretty soon my quaint little penitentiary had turned into one of those for-profit prisons that people see on TV or YouTube and get mad about. This game taught me about the dangers of for-profit prisons more than any statistic or documentary could, and that's because it let me see first hand how the incentives of the prison system force prisons to treat their inmates poorly and overcrowd the space that they have. This game's message and it's ability to teach  are what really turn this game from really good to great in my opinion, and I give Introversion the highest praises for tackling this issue with the respect and insight that it truly deserves.

This review is getting pretty long now, so I'll wrap it up with a quick list of pros and cons.

Pros:
- Excellent management mechanics
- Great replay value
- Difficult yet fair
- Insightful message
- Educational (Somewhat)

Cons:
- Lack of polish
- Escape mode not very fleshed out
- Experimental map settings leave a lot to be desired

TL;DR if you like management games this is a must buy. everything you'd want in a city builder with an intriguing theme to boot. 9/10

[h1]I'm a Time-Travelling Dictator[/h1]

I have to ration how often I load this game, as I'll start playing it and then wonder how I've invented time travel, 6 hours passing in the blink of an eye. It also made me realize I'm a bit of a cruel dictator when it comes to human rights. I build the smallest possible, cramped yet efficient rooms, give the bare necessities in visitation and entertainment, lock up prisoners who complain and make the rest work 10 hours a day, all whilst banking fat cash into my account and cackling maniacally.

[h1]An In-Depth Simulation[/h1]

This is a somewhat realistic simulation of the basics of human life in a prison. Each prisoner has needs, and you have to meet those needs by building a variety of rooms and filling them with objects. It sounds simple, but the gameplay is fairly complex, with emotional, psychological and physical needs all coming into play.

The mechanics are straight forward seeming, but it's easy for riots to start and things to escalate wildly out of hand. Oops, turns out people reeeeally don't like it if you don't feed them. There is a deceptive amount of strategy and forward thinking required that makes each prison you create more efficient as you build up your knowledge. My first one burned to the ground and resulted in a few dozen guards getting shanked whilst the prisoers escaped... yeah okay, not only should I have fed them, I guess I should have built prison walls too. Live and learn (unless you're a guard in Prison Athravan, RIP!)

Add to this research trees, staff management, educational and recreational programs, managing addiction, guard rotas and pathing, shakedowns and security, visitation, resources and financial stress and you have one hell of a deep simulation game.

[h1]Modding Community[/h1]

On top of the pretty much endless simulation, the modding community for this game is fantastic. Thousands of people have poured their heart into prison and object design, as well as scenarios and additional features, and it's all available free. The game was great to begin with, but kudos to all those who have submitted to the workshop, and to the developers for providing the tools for the people who are way smarter than me to share their creations. All I can do is scroll through page after page in awe of their dedication and skill.

[h1]TL:DR A game that may look simple on the surface but has an absolute ton of depth. An extremely well built simulation game; with the added bonus of a very active and creative modding community to boot. Big thumbs up![/h1]
